title: Relative electrical charges of subatomic particles

notes.definition: Atoms contain protons (relative charge +1), neutrons (0) and electrons (−1). An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so it has no overall charge, and the number of protons is its atomic number.
explanation: In the nuclear model, an atom has a tiny central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons arranged in shells (energy levels) around it. The three subatomic particles have different relative electrical charges: a proton has a charge of +1, a neutron has a charge of 0 (it is neutral), and an electron has a charge of −1. These are relative charges: the charge on an electron is exactly equal in size but opposite in sign to the charge on a proton.

In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus. The total positive charge of the protons is therefore exactly cancelled by the total negative charge of the electrons, so atoms have no overall electrical charge. Neutrons do not affect the overall charge because they have no charge. For example, a lithium atom has 3 protons (total charge +3) and 3 electrons (total charge −3), so its overall charge is 0.

The number of protons in an atom of an element is called its atomic number. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons, and atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons. This means the number of protons identifies the element: every atom with 6 protons is carbon, every atom with 11 protons is sodium, and an atom with 12 protons must be magnesium. The periodic table lists elements in order of atomic number.

Because the number of electrons equals the number of protons in an atom, you can work out the number of electrons from the atomic number. Chlorine has atomic number 17, so a chlorine atom has 17 protons and 17 electrons. If a particle has different numbers of protons and electrons, it is not a neutral atom: it has an overall charge and is called an ion. Its charge is found by adding the relative charges, for example 11 protons (+11) and 10 electrons (−10) give an overall charge of +1.

The negatively charged electrons are attracted to the positively charged nucleus because opposite charges attract. This attraction holds the electrons in the atom. You should be able to use the nuclear model to describe any atom: state the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus, the number of electrons around it, and explain why the atom is neutral.
keyFacts: Proton: relative charge +1, found in the nucleus.
Neutron: relative charge 0, found in the nucleus.
Electron: relative charge −1, found in shells around the nucleus.
In an atom, number of electrons = number of protons.
Atoms have no overall charge because the positive and negative charges cancel.
All atoms of the same element have the same number of protons.
Atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons.
Overall charge of a particle = (number of protons) − (number of electrons).

keyTerms.definition: A subatomic particle in the nucleus with a relative charge of +1.
A subatomic particle in the nucleus with no charge (relative charge 0).
A subatomic particle in shells around the nucleus with a relative charge of −1.
The tiny centre of an atom, containing protons and neutrons.
The number of protons in an atom of an element.
The charge of a particle compared with the charge on a proton (+1).
A charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms gains or loses electrons.

equations.name: Number of electrons in an atom
equations.formula: number of electrons = number of protons = atomic number

equations.name: Overall charge of a particle
equations.formula: overall charge = number of protons − number of electrons

workedExamples.title: Electrons from atomic number
workedExamples.question: Calcium has atomic number 20. How many protons and electrons are in a calcium atom?
steps: Atomic number = number of protons, so there are 20 protons.
In an atom, number of electrons = number of protons, so there are 20 electrons.

workedExamples.title: Working out overall charge
workedExamples.question: A particle contains 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 10 electrons. What is its overall charge, and is it an atom?
steps: Neutrons have no charge, so they add 0.
workedExamples.answer: The overall charge is 2−, so it is not a neutral atom; it is an ion (an oxide ion, O²⁻, since 8 protons means oxygen).

workedExamples.title: Identifying an element
workedExamples.question: An atom has 14 electrons. Identify the element.
steps: In an atom, number of protons = number of electrons = 14.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think neutrons are negative because they are 'opposite' to protons.
misconceptions.right: In fact neutrons have no charge. Electrons are the negative particles.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the atomic number is the number of protons plus neutrons.
misconceptions.right: In fact the atomic number is only the number of protons. Protons plus neutrons is the mass number.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and neutrons.
misconceptions.right: In fact an atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons. The number of neutrons does not affect charge.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think atoms of the same element can have different numbers of protons.
misconceptions.right: In fact all atoms of an element have the same number of protons; changing the number of protons changes the element.

realWorld: Static electricity, such as a balloon sticking to a wall, happens when electrons (negative) are transferred between materials, leaving one positively charged.
Mass spectrometers and particle detectors use the charges of particles to steer them with electric and magnetic fields.
Scientists confirm the discovery of a new element by showing that its atoms have a number of protons that no known element has.
examTips: Learn the table: proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1. Write the signs; a charge of 1 for an electron without the minus sign will not get the mark.
When explaining why atoms are neutral, mention both equal numbers of protons and electrons and that their charges are equal and opposite.
Use the periodic table: the atomic number (the smaller number) gives the number of protons and, for an atom, the number of electrons.
If the numbers of protons and electrons differ, the particle is an ion: more protons means positive, more electrons means negative.
summary: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are in shells.
In an atom, number of electrons equals number of protons.
Atomic number is the number of protons.
All atoms of an element have the same number of protons; different elements have different numbers.

markScheme: 1 mark: +1
questions.explanation: A proton has a relative charge of +1. An electron is −1 and a neutron is 0.

questions.question: What is the relative charge of a neutron?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0
questions.explanation: Neutrons are neutral, which is where their name comes from. Students sometimes wrongly think neutrons are negative.

questions.question: What is the relative charge of an electron?
markScheme: 1 mark: −1
questions.explanation: Electrons are negative, with a charge equal in size and opposite in sign to a proton's.

Electrons only

options: They have equal numbers of protons and neutrons
Neutrons cancel out the charge of the protons
They have equal numbers of protons and electrons
Electrons have no charge
markScheme: 1 mark: they have equal numbers of protons and electrons
questions.explanation: Each proton (+1) is balanced by an electron (−1). Neutrons have no charge, so they cannot cancel anything.

questions.question: An atom has 11 protons. Which element is it?
options: Sodium
Neon
Magnesium
Potassium
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium
questions.explanation: Atomic number 11 is sodium. Neon is 10, magnesium is 12 and potassium is 19.

questions.question: Which statement about atoms is correct?
options: All atoms of an element have the same number of neutrons
All atoms of an element have the same number of protons
Atoms of different elements can have the same number of protons
The number of electrons in an atom equals the number of neutrons
markScheme: 1 mark: all atoms of an element have the same number of protons
questions.explanation: The number of protons defines the element. Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons (isotopes).

questions.question: Atom X has atomic number 8 and atom Y has atomic number 9. What can you conclude?
options: X and Y are the same element
X and Y have the same number of electrons
X has more protons than Y
X and Y are different elements
markScheme: 1 mark: X and Y are different elements
questions.explanation: Different numbers of protons means different elements (X is oxygen, Y is fluorine). Y has more protons and electrons than X.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the numbers of subatomic particles in a particle.
What is the overall charge of the particle?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2+
questions.explanation: Overall charge = 12 − 10 = +2. Neutrons have no charge, so they are ignored. A 2− answer comes from subtracting the wrong way round.

questions.question:
Chlorine has atomic number 17.
Give the number of electrons in a chlorine atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: 17
questions.explanation: Atomic number = number of protons = 17, and in an atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

questions.question:
An atom contains 20 electrons.
Give the atomic number of this atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: 20
questions.explanation: In an atom, protons = electrons = 20, and the atomic number is the number of protons. The element is calcium.

questions.question:
Oxygen has atomic number 8.
Determine the total relative charge of all the protons in the nucleus of an oxygen atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: +8
questions.explanation: There are 8 protons, each +1, giving a total of +8. The neutrons add no charge.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the numbers of subatomic particles in a particle.
Calculate the overall relative charge of the particle.
markScheme: 1 mark: −1
questions.explanation: Overall charge = 9 − 10 = −1. The neutrons have no charge, so they do not count. This particle is a fluoride ion, F⁻.

questions.question:
Aluminium has atomic number 13.
An aluminium atom loses 3 electrons.
Determine the number of electrons the particle now has.
markScheme: 1 mark: 10
questions.explanation: The atom starts with 13 electrons (equal to 13 protons). 13 − 3 = 10 electrons. The overall charge is now +3.

questions.question:
Sulfur has atomic number 16.
A sulfur atom gains 2 electrons.
Calculate the overall relative charge of the particle formed.
markScheme: 1 mark: electrons = 16 + 2 = 18
1 mark: charge = 16 − 18 = −2
questions.explanation: The particle has 16 protons (+16) and 18 electrons (−18), so the overall charge is −2. It is a sulfide ion, S²⁻.

questions.question: Complete Table 1 to show the relative charge of each subatomic particle.
markScheme: 1 mark: proton +1
1 mark: neutron 0
1 mark: electron −1
questions.explanation: Signs matter: the electron's charge must be written as −1.

questions.question: What is meant by the atomic number of an element?
markScheme: 1 mark: the number of protons in an atom (of that element)
questions.explanation: Atomic number is the number of protons. It is not the number of protons plus neutrons.

questions.question: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
acceptedAnswers: equal numbers of protons and electrons
same number of protons and electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: number of protons equals number of electrons
1 mark: protons are +1 and electrons are −1, so the charges cancel
questions.explanation: The answer must mention electrons, not neutrons, and explain that the charges are equal and opposite.

questions.question: State how atoms of different elements differ from each other.
markScheme: 1 mark: they have different numbers of protons (different atomic numbers)
questions.explanation: The number of protons is unique to each element.

questions.question: Carbon has atomic number 6. Use the nuclear model to describe a carbon atom with 6 neutrons.
markScheme: 1 mark: a nucleus containing 6 protons and 6 neutrons
1 mark: 6 electrons
1 mark: electrons in shells (energy levels) around the nucleus
questions.explanation: Atomic number 6 means 6 protons, so a neutral atom has 6 electrons. The neutrons are in the nucleus with the protons.

questions.question: An atom has 15 protons. Name the element and state the number of electrons in the atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: phosphorus
1 mark: 15 electrons
questions.explanation: Atomic number 15 is phosphorus (P). A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons.

questions.question: Explain why the number of neutrons in an atom does not affect its overall charge.
markScheme: 1 mark: neutrons have no charge (relative charge 0)
questions.explanation: Only protons and electrons carry charge.

questions.question: A student says: "Some sodium atoms have 11 protons and some have 12 protons." Explain why the student is wrong.
acceptedAnswers: number of protons defines the element
markScheme: 1 mark: all atoms of an element (sodium) have the same number of protons (11)
1 mark: an atom with 12 protons would be a different element (magnesium)
questions.explanation: The student may be confusing protons with neutrons. Sodium atoms can differ in neutrons but never in protons.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the numbers of protons and electrons in a particle.
Explain whether this particle is an atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: it is not an atom, because the numbers of protons and electrons are not equal
1 mark: it has an overall charge of 2− (it is an ion)
questions.explanation: Atoms are neutral. 8 protons and 10 electrons give a charge of −2, so this is an oxide ion, O²⁻.

questions.question:
Fluorine has atomic number 9. A fluorine atom contains 10 neutrons.
Describe the structure of a fluorine atom in terms of its subatomic particles, and explain why the atom has no overall charge.
markScheme: Indicative content: nucleus at the centre contains 9 protons and 10 neutrons; 9 electrons in shells around the nucleus; protons +1, neutrons 0, electrons −1; total positive charge +9, total negative charge −9; charges cancel so overall charge is 0; neutrons do not affect charge.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct numbers and locations of all three particles, with a clear explanation of neutrality using relative charges.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct numbers or locations, or a simple statement that protons and electrons are equal.
questions.explanation: Atomic number gives protons (9) and electrons (9). The neutrons (10) are given; they sit in the nucleus and carry no charge.

questions.question: Explain why scientists use the number of protons, rather than the number of neutrons or electrons, to identify which element an atom belongs to.
markScheme: Indicative content: all atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons; atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons; the number of protons is the atomic number; the number of neutrons can vary between atoms of the same element (isotopes); the number of electrons can change when atoms form ions, while the protons stay the same; so protons are the only number that is fixed for an element and unique to it.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains that the proton number is fixed and unique, and gives reasons why neutron and electron numbers are not reliable.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that each element has its own number of protons, with little further explanation.
questions.explanation: Electrons can be gained or lost and neutron numbers vary, but the number of protons never changes for a given element.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the atomic numbers of two elements, A and B.
Use the nuclear model and the relative charges of subatomic particles to describe an atom of each element.
Explain why both atoms are neutral and why they are atoms of different elements.
markScheme: Indicative content: each atom has a tiny nucleus with electrons in shells around it; A (lithium) has 3 protons in the nucleus and 3 electrons; B (sodium) has 11 protons and 11 electrons; both also contain neutrons in the nucleus, which have no charge; protons have relative charge +1, electrons −1; in each atom the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the total positive and negative charges cancel (+3 and −3; +11 and −11); A and B are different elements because they have different numbers of protons (different atomic numbers); all atoms of lithium have 3 protons and all atoms of sodium have 11.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): accurate description of both atoms with correct numbers and locations, clear explanation of neutrality using charges, and a clear reason they are different elements.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): mostly correct description of the atoms with some explanation of either neutrality or why they are different elements.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct numbers or simple statements about charges.
questions.explanation: Atomic number fixes both the identity of the element and, in an atom, the number of electrons. Neutrons are present but do not affect charge or identity.
